Definition: Attacking the person making an argument instead of addressing the argument itself. It distracts from whether the claim is true.
Example: Someone says, 'You only think that diet works because you sell diet books,' instead of discussing the evidence for the diet.
FaithDiscussionExample: In a discussion someone says, 'You only believe the Bible because you were raised in church,' instead of engaging with what the Bible actually says.
HowToRespond: Thank the person for being honest, then gently separate the messenger from the message: 'My background is part of my story — could we look together at whether the claim itself holds up?'

Definition: Misrepresenting someone's position to make it easier to attack, then arguing against the distorted version instead of their real view.
Example: Someone argues for better road safety and is accused of wanting to ban all cars, which was never what they said.
FaithDiscussionExample: A Christian who says faith and reason work together is told, 'So you think we should just believe blindly without any evidence,' which misstates their position.
HowToRespond: Restate your view calmly and check understanding: 'That is not quite what I meant — here is what I am actually saying. Does that version sound fair to discuss?'

Definition: Presenting only two options as if they are the only possibilities, when other options exist. It is also called a false dilemma.
Example: A speaker says, 'You are either with our plan completely or you want the project to fail,' ignoring middle options and compromises.
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone says, 'You must choose science or the Bible — you cannot have both,' as if thoughtful Christians have not held both together for centuries.
HowToRespond: Name the missing options with kindness: 'I wonder if there might be a third way here that honors both concerns. Could we explore it together?'

Definition: Claiming that one step will inevitably lead to an extreme outcome, without showing why each step must follow. A possible concern is treated as a certain chain reaction.
Example: A parent hears, 'If we let him stay up ten minutes later tonight, soon he will never follow any bedtime at all.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone warns, 'If you question one interpretation of a passage, soon you will not believe anything in the Bible,' without showing why careful study must lead there.
HowToRespond: Acknowledge the underlying concern, then ask for the links in the chain: 'I share your desire to stay faithful — can we look step by step at what actually follows?'

Definition: Treating a claim as true simply because an authority figure said it, especially when that person is not an expert on the topic or experts disagree.
Example: An advertisement says a toothpaste must be best because a famous actor recommends it, though the actor is not a dentist.
FaithDiscussionExample: A video claims, 'A famous scientist said the resurrection is impossible, so it is settled,' without examining the historical evidence itself.
HowToRespond: Respect expertise while asking for reasons: 'I value what experts say — could we look at the evidence and arguments they are pointing to, not just the conclusion?'

Definition: Claiming something is true because it has not been proved false, or false because it has not been proved true. Lack of evidence is treated as evidence itself.
Example: Someone says, 'No one has proved this remedy does not work, so it definitely works.'
FaithDiscussionExample: A skeptic says, 'Since you cannot prove God exists in a laboratory, God cannot exist,' and a believer might reply in reverse, 'You cannot disprove God, so that proves He exists.' Neither move is fair on its own.
HowToRespond: Agree that uncertainty is honest, then shift to what we do know: 'Not having a final proof either way invites us to weigh the evidence we actually have.'

Definition: Assuming the conclusion is already true inside the argument itself, so the reasoning goes in a circle without independent support. The claim is restated rather than proved.
Example: Someone argues, 'This book is the most reliable because it says so itself and everything it says is true.'
FaithDiscussionExample: In conversation: 'The Bible is true because it is God's Word, and we know it is God's Word because the Bible says so,' offered as the whole argument without any other reasons.
HowToRespond: Notice the circle gently and offer additional grounds: 'That states what I believe — let me also share historical and experiential reasons that support it.'

Definition: A form of begging the question where the conclusion is used to support its own premise, so A is true because of B and B is true because of A.
Example: A student says, 'Our team is the best because we are better than everyone, and we know we are better because we are the best.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone says, 'I know this interpretation is right because my teacher taught it, and I know my teacher is always right because he taught this interpretation.'
HowToRespond: Unpack the loop together without embarrassment: 'It sounds like we are using the same idea twice — is there an outside reason or passage we can test it against?'

Definition: Judging a claim true or false based only on where it came from — its origin, history, or source — instead of its merits.
Example: A helpful idea is dismissed with, 'That suggestion came from the new employee, so it cannot be any good.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone says, 'The Bible cannot be trusted because it was written by ancient people,' judging the message only by its age and authors rather than its content and evidence.
HowToRespond: Affirm that origins can raise good questions, then return to content: 'Ancient does not automatically mean untrue — could we examine what it says and the evidence for it?'

Definition: Redefining a group on the spot to exclude a counterexample, so the original claim can never be challenged. The definition moves whenever evidence appears.
Example: After hearing of a kind Scotsman who disproves a stereotype, someone replies, 'Well, no true Scotsman would act that way.'
FaithDiscussionExample: When a professing Christian behaves badly, someone says, 'No true Christian would ever do that,' instead of honestly acknowledging failure and the need for repentance.
HowToRespond: Be honest about real examples: 'Christians, like everyone, can fail badly. Rather than redefine the word, let us look at what Christ actually calls His followers to be.'

Definition: Introducing an unrelated topic to distract from the original issue, so the conversation drifts away without answering the question at hand.
Example: When asked about a missed deadline, an employee starts talking at length about how unfair the office parking is.
FaithDiscussionExample: Asked about a difficult Bible passage, someone changes the subject entirely: 'Well, what about all the bad things done in the name of religion?' — an important topic, but a different one.
HowToRespond: Honor the new topic while returning kindly: 'That is worth discussing too. Could we finish this question first, then come back to that one together?'

Definition: Answering a criticism by accusing the other person of the same thing — 'you do it too' — instead of addressing whether the criticism is true. It is a form of appeal to hypocrisy.
Example: A driver caught speeding says, 'You speed sometimes too, so you have no right to say anything.'
FaithDiscussionExample: When the church is challenged on generosity, a reply comes, 'Well, secular charities waste money too,' which does not answer how the church itself should give.
HowToRespond: Own what is true first: 'You may be right that we fall short too — that is something we should fix. Can we still look at the original point on its own?'

Definition: Trying to win agreement by stirring strong feelings — fear, pity, anger, or guilt — instead of offering reasons and evidence.
Example: An advert says, 'If you really loved your family, you would buy this product today,' using guilt rather than facts about the product.
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone says, 'How could a loving person ever believe in judgment? That idea just feels cruel,' letting a strong feeling settle a theological question by itself.
HowToRespond: Take feelings seriously without letting them decide alone: 'I understand why that feels hard — I feel it too. Could we look slowly at what Scripture teaches and why?'

Definition: Drawing a broad conclusion from too small or unrepresentative a sample. A few examples are treated as proof about a whole group.
Example: After meeting two rude tourists, someone declares, 'Everyone from that country is rude.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone meets two disinterested church members and concludes, 'Christians never really care about anyone outside their group,' based on a very narrow experience.
HowToRespond: Validate the experience, then widen the picture: 'I am sorry that was your experience. Would you be open to meeting other examples before we settle on the whole group?'

Definition: Assuming that because one event followed another, the first must have caused the second. The Latin means 'after this, therefore because of this.'
Example: A player wears lucky socks, the team wins, and he concludes the socks caused the victory.
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone prays for a job, receives an offer the next week, and while gratitude is fitting, a friend might too quickly claim prayer always works like a formula for getting what we want.
HowToRespond: Celebrate good outcomes while staying careful about causes: 'I am thankful for how this turned out. Let us be thoughtful about what we can and cannot claim caused it.'

Definition: Using the same word in two different senses within one argument, so the conclusion appears to follow when it does not. The meaning shifts midway.
Example: Someone argues, 'A mouse needs cheese, and this computer mouse is a mouse, so it needs cheese,' shifting between animal and device.
FaithDiscussionExample: In a faith talk, 'faith' shifts between 'trust based on reasons' and 'believing without any reason,' so a claim about blind belief is used to dismiss trusting faith.
HowToRespond: Define terms together early: 'We may be using that word differently — could we pause and agree on what we each mean by it here?'

Definition: Asking a question that smuggles in an unproved assumption, so any direct yes-or-no answer accepts that assumption.
Example: A reporter asks, 'Have you stopped wasting company money?' — answering either yes or no admits there was waste to begin with.
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone asks a pastor, 'Why does your church keep brainwashing young people?' — the question assumes manipulation before any evidence is discussed.
HowToRespond: Unpack the assumption politely before answering: 'There is an assumption tucked into that question — could we look at whether it is accurate first, then I will gladly answer?'

Definition: Changing the standard of proof after the original standard has been met, so the other side can never succeed. The target keeps shifting.
Example: A manager asks for ten sales, gets ten, then says only twenty would really prove the employee is doing well.
FaithDiscussionExample: A skeptic asks for one good manuscript reason to trust a Gospel, is given several, then says none of it counts unless there is video evidence from the first century.
HowToRespond: Name the original standard with grace: 'We started with that first request — since we have looked at it, could we agree on what would count as a fair next step?'

Definition: Claiming something is true or good because many people are joining in or doing it right now. Popular momentum is treated as proof.
Example: An advert urges, 'Everyone is switching to this phone — do not be left behind,' without comparing the phones themselves.
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone says, 'This new spiritual trend is everywhere online, so it must be true and good for you,' based on how fast it is spreading.
HowToRespond: Slow the momentum kindly: 'It is understandable to notice what is trending. Could we ask whether it is true and wise, apart from how popular it feels right now?'

Definition: Assuming that because something is natural it must be good, or because something is unnatural it must be bad, without further moral reasoning.
Example: Someone claims, 'This supplement must be safe and better because it is all-natural,' though some natural substances are harmful.
FaithDiscussionExample: In an ethics discussion someone says, 'That behavior occurs in nature, so it must be morally right for people,' skipping the step of asking what God intends for human flourishing.
HowToRespond: Appreciate creation while asking the deeper question: 'Nature teaches us a lot, but could we also ask what is good and purposeful, not only what occurs naturally?'
RelatedTopics: Christian Ethics; Logic; Nature and Creation

Definition: Treating widespread belief as evidence of truth — if most people believe it, it must be right. It is closely related to the bandwagon, but focuses on belief rather than behavior.
Example: A student argues, 'Most people in our class think this answer is right, so it must be the correct one.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone says, 'Millions of people no longer believe the Bible is relevant, so it clearly is not,' or the reverse, 'So many people believe it, that alone proves it true.' Both rely on numbers alone.
HowToRespond: Respect people on all sides while returning to reasons: 'Numbers tell us what is common, not always what is true — could we weigh the actual claims together?'

Definition: Mistaking a connection between two things for proof that one caused the other, when they may be linked by coincidence or a third factor. It includes post hoc reasoning but is broader.
Example: Ice cream sales and sunburn both rise in summer, so someone wrongly concludes ice cream causes sunburn, missing the sun as the common cause.
FaithDiscussionExample: A decline in church attendance and a social problem rise in the same decade, and someone blames one for the other without checking other causes or evidence.
HowToRespond: Look for other explanations together: 'They do rise together — could there be a third factor, or a different connection, that explains both more fairly?'

Definition: Using a single personal story or vivid example as proof for a broad claim, instead of wider evidence. Stories illuminate, but one story rarely settles a pattern.
Example: Someone says, 'My grandfather smoked every day and lived to 95, so smoking cannot be harmful.'
FaithDiscussionExample: A person says, 'I prayed once and nothing happened, so prayer never works,' or, 'My friend had a powerful experience, so that proves every claim about that teaching.'
HowToRespond: Honor the story, then place it in context: 'Your experience matters and I want to hear it. Could we also look at the wider picture and what Scripture shows over time?'

Definition: Selecting only the evidence that supports a preferred conclusion while ignoring evidence that points the other way. It is also called selective evidence.
Example: A review quotes one positive sentence from a mostly critical review and presents it as if the reviewer loved the product.
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone quotes a single verse about judgment to prove God is only angry, ignoring the many passages about His mercy — or quotes only comfort verses and ignores calls to repentance.
HowToRespond: Invite the whole picture: 'That passage is important — could we read it in context and alongside the other passages on this topic, so we hear the full counsel?'

Definition: Finding a pattern in random or selected data after the fact, then treating that pattern as if it was the target all along — like painting the target around bullet holes.
Example: A gambler notices he won on three Tuesdays and declares Tuesdays are his lucky winning pattern, ignoring all the Tuesdays he lost.
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone collects scattered numbers and dates from unrelated passages after an event and presents them as a precise prophecy of that event, having chosen only the fitting pieces afterward.
HowToRespond: Ask what was predicted beforehand: 'That is an interesting pattern — was it identified before the event, and does it hold up when we include the pieces that do not fit?'

Definition: Assuming something is better or truer simply because it is new, modern, or recent. Newness alone is not evidence.
Example: An advert claims, 'This is the newest model, so it must be the best choice for everyone,' without comparing features.
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone dismisses historic Christian teaching with, 'That belief is centuries old — it is time we moved past it,' as if age alone proved it wrong.
HowToRespond: Welcome fresh insight while testing it: 'New ideas can be a gift. Could we judge this one by its truth and fruit, rather than by its date?'

Definition: Assuming something is right or better simply because it has long been done or believed that way. Tradition can carry wisdom, but longevity alone is not proof.
Example: A workplace resists a helpful change with, 'We have always done it this way, so this way must be best.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone says, 'Our church has always interpreted this passage this way, so there is no need to ever re-examine it,' closing the door on careful study of the text itself.
HowToRespond: Honor tradition as a starting point: 'Tradition often preserves real wisdom — could we also test our practice against Scripture together, as earlier generations did?'

Definition: Assuming that what is true of the parts must be true of the whole. A quality of individual pieces is transferred to the group without justification.
Example: Someone reasons, 'Every player on this team is excellent, so the team as a whole must play excellently together,' ignoring teamwork and chemistry.
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'Each verse in this chapter is encouraging, so the whole Bible must never contain anything challenging or hard,' moving from a part to the whole too quickly.
HowToRespond: Distinguish parts and whole gently: 'That may be true of the parts — could we check whether it still holds when we consider the whole together?'

Definition: Assuming that what is true of the whole must be true of each part. It is the reverse of composition, dividing a group quality down to every member.
Example: A famous university is assumed to mean every single student there must be brilliant in every subject.
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone says, 'The early church was generous, so every individual early Christian must have been generous in every way,' flattening a general description into a claim about each person.
HowToRespond: Keep the whole and the parts distinct: 'A true description of the group does not always describe each member — could we look at the individuals on their own evidence?'

Definition: Assuming the truth must lie halfway between two opposing positions simply because it is the compromise. Sometimes one side is right, sometimes the middle is, but splitting the difference is not proof.
Example: Two people disagree on a factual bill amount — one says $100, the other $0 despite a receipt for $100 — and someone insists the fair answer must be $50.
FaithDiscussionExample: In a doctrinal disagreement, someone says, 'One side says Jesus rose bodily and the other says He did not, so the truth is probably somewhere in between,' treating a factual claim as a compromise.
HowToRespond: Seek truth over symmetry: 'Compromise can be kind in preferences, but for factual claims could we follow the evidence, even if it lands closer to one side?'

Definition: An invalid deductive form: if P then Q; Q is true; therefore P must be true. The consequent being true does not prove the antecedent, since something else could cause Q.
Example: Someone argues, 'If it rains, the grass is wet. The grass is wet, so it must have rained' — forgetting the sprinkler could explain it.
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'If God is real, people experience peace. I feel peace, so God must be real' — the feeling is real, but other causes of peace exist too.
HowToRespond: Honor the experience, then ask for independent support: 'That peace matters — could we also look for reasons that point the same way on their own?'

Definition: An invalid deductive form: if P then Q; P is false; therefore Q must be false. Denying the antecedent does not deny the consequent, since Q could hold for other reasons.
Example: Someone argues, 'If you study, you will pass. You did not study, so you will fail' — though you might pass anyway.
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'If someone truly believes, they never doubt. She doubts, so she does not believe' — though doubt and faith often live together.
HowToRespond: Test the first claim itself: 'Doubt and faith often live together — let's check whether never doubting is really the mark of belief.'

Definition: An invalid syllogism: all A are B; C is B; therefore C is A. Sharing a property with a group does not place something inside that group.
Example: Someone argues, 'All birds have wings. Bats have wings, so bats are birds.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'All Christians pray. He prays, so he must be a Christian' — prayer alone does not establish it.
HowToRespond: Name the gap gently: 'That shows a shared trait, not the same group — what else would confirm it?'

Definition: An invalid syllogism: all A are B; no C is A; therefore no C is B. The conclusion reaches further than the premises allow, because C could still be B another way.
Example: Someone argues, 'All dogs are mammals. No cats are dogs, so no cats are mammals.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'All prophets spoke for God. No poet is a prophet, so no poet speaks for God' — though poets can still speak truthfully about God.
HowToRespond: Show the overreach: 'The conclusion goes further than the premises allow — let's see what actually follows.'

Definition: An invalid syllogism: all A are B; all A are C; therefore all C are B. The minor term is distributed in the conclusion but not in the premises.
Example: Someone argues, 'All cats are mammals. All cats are four-legged, so all four-legged things are mammals.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'All apostles were Jews. All apostles were men, so all Jewish men are apostles.'
HowToRespond: Flip it to expose the error: 'By that pattern, every shared trait would prove membership — let's check the direction.'

Definition: Concluding that something exists merely because a universal claim is true. 'All A are B' does not by itself prove that any A exists.
Example: Someone argues, 'All unicorns have horns, so some unicorn has a horn.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'All flawless Bible translations agree, so a flawless translation exists' — the universal claim alone does not prove one exists.
HowToRespond: Ask for the extra step: 'A universal claim doesn't by itself prove something exists — what separate evidence shows it does?'

Definition: An invalid syllogism: a negative premise ('no A is B') combined with another premise cannot yield an affirmative conclusion ('some C is B').
Example: Someone argues, 'No fish are mammals. Some pets are fish, so some pets are mammals.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'No work earns salvation. Some church activities are works, so some church activities earn salvation' — the form cannot carry that conclusion.
Fallacy: Affirmative Conclusion from a Negative Premise
HowToRespond: Point to the form, not the faith: 'A negative premise can't yield that positive conclusion — let's rebuild the argument.'

Definition: An invalid syllogism: two affirmative premises cannot yield a negative conclusion. If all A are B and all C are A, then all C are B — not none.
Example: Someone argues, 'All cats are mammals. All Siamese are cats, so no Siamese are mammals.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'All believers are forgiven. All new believers are believers, so no new believers are forgiven' — the premises actually point the other way.
HowToRespond: Follow the premises to their real conclusion: 'Affirmative premises can't prove a negative — they actually point the other way here.'

Definition: Drawing a conclusion from two negative premises. Two 'no' statements together prove nothing about the relationship between the remaining terms.
Example: Someone argues, 'No birds are fish. No penguins are fish, so penguins are not birds' — yet penguins are birds.
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'No angel is human. No demon is human, so demons are not angels' — yet demons are fallen angels.
HowToRespond: Note the shared gap: 'Two negatives leave the connection open — we'd need a positive premise to settle it.'

Definition: Illegitimately converting 'all A are B' into 'all B are A'. Conversion works for 'some' and 'no' statements, but not for universal affirmatives.
Example: Someone argues, 'All roses are flowers, so all flowers are roses.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'All prayers in the Bible are inspired, so all inspired words are prayers in the Bible.'
HowToRespond: Keep the direction straight: 'Conversion only works one way for all-statements — let's not flip it.'

Definition: Illegitimately moving from 'every A has some B' to 'there is some B that fits every A'. Each person having something does not mean one thing serves everyone.
Example: Someone argues, 'Every student has a favorite teacher, so there is one teacher who is every student's favorite.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'Every believer has a spiritual gift, so there is one gift every believer has.'
HowToRespond: Separate the two claims: 'Each person having something doesn't mean one thing serves everyone.'

Definition: Confusing the necessity of a whole conditional with the necessity of its consequent. 'Necessarily, if P then Q' does not mean 'if P, then necessarily Q'.
Example: Someone argues, 'It is necessarily true that if I am sitting, I am seated — so if I am sitting, I am necessarily seated.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'If God knows what I will do, then I must necessarily do it' — but the 'must' belongs to the whole statement, not to the person choosing.
HowToRespond: Move the 'must' back where it belongs: 'Knowledge of what someone freely chooses doesn't force the choice.'

Definition: Substituting co-referring terms inside a belief or knowledge context, where recognition matters. Not recognizing someone under one description does not change who they are.
Example: Someone argues, 'You know your father, but you do not know the masked man — so the masked man is not your father.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'The disciples did not recognize the risen Jesus at first, so the man with them was not Jesus' — yet recognition is not identity.
HowToRespond: Separate knowing from being: 'Not recognizing someone under one description doesn't change who they are.'

Definition: Arguing 'A or B; A; therefore not B' when the 'or' is not exclusive. Unless the options genuinely exclude each other, one being true does not rule out the other.
Example: Someone argues, 'You can have tea or coffee. You chose tea, so you cannot have coffee.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'Worship can be in spirit or in truth. This service worships in spirit, so it cannot be in truth' — yet John 4:24 joins both.
HowToRespond: Check the 'or': "'Or' often means 'and/or' — could both be true together here?"

Definition: Trying to win an argument by threat rather than evidence: agree, or face a penalty. A threat may be real, but it is not a reason the claim is true.
Example: Someone argues, 'Support this policy or you will lose your job.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'Accept my interpretation, or I will tell everyone you are a heretic.'
HowToRespond: Name it kindly and return to reasons: 'A threat isn't evidence — could we discuss the reasons themselves?'

Definition: Urging belief because of sad circumstances rather than evidence. Suffering can show sincerity, but sincerity does not settle truth.
Example: Someone argues, 'This product must be good — the inventor lost everything making it.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'This teaching must be true — the preacher suffered so much for it.'
HowToRespond: Honor the suffering, then weigh the claim: 'Suffering can show sincerity, but let's weigh the evidence too.'

Definition: Rejecting a claim because its consequences would be unpleasant, or accepting one because its consequences are welcome. How we feel about a conclusion does not decide whether it is true.
Example: Someone argues, 'Free will cannot be an illusion — that would make morality meaningless.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'Hell cannot be real — that would be too terrible.'
HowToRespond: Separate feeling from fact: 'How we feel about a conclusion doesn't decide whether it's true — let's look at the grounds.'

Definition: Discrediting a claim because of who else holds it, rather than engaging its reasons. A claim stands or falls on its own merits, not on its neighbors.
Example: Someone argues, 'That diet must be wrong — a celebrity criminal endorses it.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'That doctrine must be wrong — a cult also teaches something like it.'
HowToRespond: Return to the claim itself: 'A claim stands or falls on its own reasons, not on its neighbors.'

Definition: Treating wealth or success as proof of correctness. Success can come many ways, and it does not validate every opinion of the successful.
Example: Someone argues, 'He is a billionaire, so his health advice must be sound.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'That ministry is huge and wealthy, so its teaching must be correct.'
HowToRespond: Test the teaching, not the treasury: 'Success can come many ways — let's test the teaching itself.'

Definition: Treating poverty, smallness, or obscurity as proof of correctness. Being small or persecuted does not by itself make a claim true.
Example: Someone argues, 'This small unknown brand must be better — the big companies are corrupt.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'That tiny persecuted group must have the truth — the big churches are compromised.'
HowToRespond: Apply one standard to all sizes: 'Smallness isn't proof either — let's examine the claims.'

Definition: Answering a criticism by pointing at someone else's fault instead of addressing the criticism. A form of deflection closely related to tu quoque, aimed at changing the subject rather than answering.
Example: Someone argues, 'Our factory pollutes — but what about the factory across town?'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'Yes, Christians have failed here — but what about what atheists did?'
HowToRespond: Acknowledge both, then stay on topic: 'The other failure may be real, but it doesn't answer this one — let's deal with each honestly.'

Definition: Preemptively discrediting a source so that nothing they say counts, before they have even made their case. Unlike ordinary ad hominem, it poisons the well in advance.
Example: Someone argues, 'Don't listen to him — he's just a paid shill,' before he has spoken a word.
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'Don't read that scholar — he's an atheist, so nothing he says about the Bible counts.'
HowToRespond: Insist on a hearing: "Let's hear the argument first and judge it on its merits."

Definition: Treating the absence of a mention as evidence that something did not happen or is not true. Silence is only weak evidence, and only when a mention would be expected.
Example: Someone argues, 'The report never mentions safety problems, so there were none.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'The Gospels never record Jesus laughing, so Jesus never laughed.'
HowToRespond: Ask what silence can carry: "Silence isn't evidence unless we'd expect a mention — and even then it's weak."

Definition: Assuming someone is wrong, then explaining psychologically why they believe it, instead of showing the error. Motives do not settle truth, even when the motives are correctly described.
Example: Someone argues, 'You only oppose this policy because you fear change.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'You only believe in God because you need a crutch.'
HowToRespond: Return to reasons: 'Even if motives were as claimed, motives don't settle truth — let's examine the reasons.'

Definition: Using fear as a substitute for evidence. Fear can warn us, but a scary outcome does not prove a claim true or false.
Example: Someone argues, 'If you don't buy this alarm, burglars will target your home.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'If you question this teaching, you will lose your salvation.'
HowToRespond: Separate warning from proof: 'Fear can warn us, but it can't prove a claim — what are the reasons?'

Definition: Mocking a claim instead of refuting it. Laughter at a position is not an argument against it.
Example: Someone argues, 'Believing that is like believing the moon is cheese — absurd!'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'You believe a virgin had a baby? Come on.'
HowToRespond: Ask for the real objection: "Mockery isn't an argument — what's the actual objection?"

Definition: A conclusion that simply does not follow from its premises — no stated connection, just a leap. Specific forms of this leap have their own entries elsewhere in this collection.
Example: Someone argues, 'She is a great singer, so she would make a great mayor.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'He knows Greek, so his theology must be right.'
HowToRespond: Ask for the missing link: 'The conclusion may be true, but it needs its own support — what connects these?'

Definition: Ambiguity arising from sentence structure rather than from a single word's meaning. The grammar itself allows two readings, and the argument leans on only one.
Example: Someone argues from 'I saw the man with the telescope' without saying who held the telescope.
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone quotes 'Judge not' to mean never discern anything, leaning on one possible reading of the sentence rather than its context.
HowToRespond: Pause on the structure: 'When a sentence can be read two ways, let's check the context before building on one reading.'

Definition: A change of meaning produced by emphasis. Stressing different words in the same sentence can smuggle in a meaning the words alone do not carry.
Example: Someone stresses 'We should NOT trust him' versus 'We SHOULD not trust him' — the emphasis shifts what is being denied.
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone stresses 'all' in 'all have sinned' to mean every single act is sin, rather than that all people stand in need of grace.
HowToRespond: Read it plainly: "Emphasis can smuggle in a meaning the words don't carry — let's read the whole sentence plainly."

Definition: Winning an argument by defining a key term in a way that already assumes the conclusion. The definition does the arguing instead of the evidence.
Example: Someone argues, 'Real freedom means doing whatever you want, so laws destroy freedom.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'True faith means never doubting, so doubters have no faith.'
HowToRespond: Agree definitions first: "Let's agree on definitions from shared usage, not from the conclusion we want."

Definition: Treating two unequal things as if they were equivalent, so that what holds for one is assumed to hold for the other. The comparison hides a difference in weight.
Example: Someone argues, 'Skipping a workout and skipping heart medicine are both just missing a dose.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'Doubting one doctrine and rejecting the whole faith are the same thing.'
HowToRespond: Compare like with like: 'These differ in weight — let's compare like with like.'

Definition: An analogy that breaks at the very point it needs to hold. Analogies prove only through the points that genuinely match.
Example: Someone argues, 'The brain is like a computer, so it must have a delete key.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'God is like a father, so God must get tired like fathers do.'
HowToRespond: Find the break: 'Analogies prove by the points that match — where does this one break?'

Definition: Exempting your own case from a standard you apply to others, without justification for the exception. If the standard binds others, the exception needs its own reason.
Example: Someone argues, 'Everyone should cite sources — except me, because I am an expert.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'Every claim needs reasons — except my favorite preacher's, because he is anointed.'
HowToRespond: Ask for the justification: 'If the standard applies to others, what justifies the exception here?'

Definition: Demanding that others disprove your claim instead of supporting it yourself. Whoever makes the claim carries the case for it.
Example: Someone argues, 'Prove unicorns don't exist!'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'Prove God doesn't exist!'
HowToRespond: Return the burden kindly: 'Whoever makes the claim carries the case — let's hear the positive reasons.'

Definition: Treating repetition as proof. Saying a claim again, louder or more often, adds no evidence for it.
Example: Someone argues, 'It's true, it's true, it's just true.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'This interpretation is obviously right — everyone knows it.'
HowToRespond: Ask for support, not volume: "Repetition isn't evidence — what supports it?"

Definition: Overwhelming an opponent with a rapid flood of weak arguments, so no single one can be answered in the time available. Quantity is used to simulate strength.
Example: Someone fires fifty flimsy reasons in two minutes and declares victory when only three get answered.
FaithDiscussionExample: A debate opponent fires twenty objections in two minutes, leaving no time to test any one properly.
HowToRespond: Slow it down: "Let's take one argument at a time and test it properly."

Definition: Offering several defenses that contradict each other, so that at least one always seems available. If the defenses cannot all be true, they cannot jointly support the claim.
Example: Someone argues, 'I never borrowed the pot; it was broken when I got it; I returned it undamaged.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'The text means this; also it means the opposite; also it means nothing at all.'
HowToRespond: Pick one: "These defenses can't all be true — which one are we actually claiming?"

Definition: Retreating from a bold, controversial claim to a trivially true one when challenged, then returning to the bold claim once the pressure passes. The modest claim is the motte; the bold one is the bailey.
Example: Someone argues, 'Everyone should live off-grid' — challenged — 'Well, nature is nice' — and later returns to off-grid living for all.
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'All other churches are apostate' — challenged — 'Well, no church is perfect' — and later returns to calling them apostate.
HowToRespond: Pin down the claim: "Let's settle which claim we're defending — the strong one or the modest one?"

Definition: Attacking the weakest real version of a position instead of its strongest. Unlike a strawman, which distorts the view, the weak man cherry-picks its feeblest genuine defender.
Example: Someone argues, 'Some flat-earther said something silly, so all skeptics of the official story are silly.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'One prosperity preacher said something foolish, so all charismatics are foolish.'
HowToRespond: Raise the standard: "Let's engage the strongest version of the view, not its weakest defender."

Definition: Concluding that a claim is false merely because the argument for it was fallacious. A bad argument does not make its conclusion false — it only means a better argument is needed.
Example: Someone argues, 'You appealed to authority, so your claim must be wrong.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'That apologetic argument had a flaw, so Christianity must be false.'
HowToRespond: Separate argument from conclusion: 'A bad argument doesn't make a conclusion false — it just means we need a better argument.'

Definition: Crediting a claim, quotation, or idea to the wrong source, then leaning on that false authority. The error is factual, but it corrupts the argument built on it.
Example: Someone argues from 'Let them eat cake,' a line Marie Antoinette never said.
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone quotes 'God helps those who help themselves' as Scripture — it is not in the Bible at all.
HowToRespond: Check the source first: "Let's check who actually said it before leaning on it."

Definition: Citing unnamed experts — 'studies show,' 'scholars agree' — with no one named and no finding cited. Anonymity makes the authority impossible to check.
Example: Someone argues, 'Studies show this works,' without naming any study.
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'Scholars agree the Gospels were written centuries later,' without naming any scholar.
HowToRespond: Ask for names: 'Which experts, and what did they actually conclude?'

Definition: Citing a genuine expert outside their field as if the expertise transferred. Authority counts only within the field it was earned in.
Example: Someone argues, 'A famous actor says this medicine works.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'A celebrity pastor's view on ancient Hebrew grammar settles it.'
HowToRespond: Check the field: "Expertise in one field doesn't transfer — what do the relevant specialists say?"

Definition: Assuming a supernatural cause merely because no natural explanation is at hand. A gap in knowledge is not evidence for any particular cause, and it must not be confused with positive arguments from evidence.
Example: Someone argues, 'Science can't explain this yet, so it must be a miracle.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'No one can explain this healing, so it proves this doctrine' — the gap alone proves no doctrine.
HowToRespond: Ask for positive reasons: "A gap in our knowledge isn't evidence for any particular cause — let's look for positive reasons."

Definition: Believing something because you would like it to be true. Comfort is not confirmation.
Example: Someone argues, 'This lottery ticket will win — I just feel it.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'This interpretation must be right — it's the most comforting one.'
HowToRespond: Test it like any claim: "Comfort isn't confirmation — let's test it like any other claim."

Definition: Judging by the survivors while ignoring the failures. The visible winners are a biased sample, because the losers are no longer around to be counted.
Example: Someone argues, 'Every successful CEO wakes at 5am, so waking at 5am causes success' — ignoring the many who woke early and failed.
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'Every thriving church uses this method, so the method guarantees thriving' — ignoring the churches that used it and closed.
HowToRespond: Count the missing: "Let's also count the cases that didn't make it."

Definition: Ignoring how common something is when judging a probability. Even an accurate test misleads when the condition itself is rare.
Example: Someone argues, 'This test is 95% accurate and you tested positive, so you are 95% likely ill' — ignoring how rare the illness is.
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues a fulfilled detail proves a prophecy, without asking how often such details come true by chance.
HowToRespond: Ask the base rate: 'How often does this happen anyway? The base rate changes the math.'

Definition: Believing a random streak must reverse — that after several of one outcome, the opposite is 'due'. Independent events owe us no correction.
Example: Someone argues, 'Five reds in a row — black is due.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'We've had three bad years, so a revival must be next.'
HowToRespond: Check independence: "Independent events don't owe us a correction."

Definition: Believing a random streak must continue — that a run of successes makes the next success more likely. Streaks happen by chance too.
Example: Someone argues, 'She has made five shots, so she cannot miss now.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'This ministry grew three years running, so it will keep growing.'
HowToRespond: Ask for the cause: 'Streaks happen by chance too — what's the underlying cause?'

Definition: Mistaking a natural return to the average for the effect of an intervention. Extreme readings drift back on their own, with or without what followed them.
Example: Someone argues, 'I scolded him and his performance improved — scolding works.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'After the fast, attendance rose — the fast caused it,' when attendance was at a low point it would likely leave anyway.
HowToRespond: Compare with a control: 'Extreme readings drift back on their own — let's compare with a control.'

Definition: Treating correlation as causation when two things occur together. 'With this, therefore because of this' — simultaneous events need a separate causal link.
Example: Someone argues, 'Towns with more churches have more crime, so churches cause crime' — population explains both.
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'Churches with guitars grow faster, so guitars cause growth.'
HowToRespond: Look for the third factor: "Two things rising together doesn't mean one causes the other — what else could explain both?"

Definition: Reducing a complex outcome to a single cause. Most big outcomes have many causes, and naming one hides the rest.
Example: Someone argues, 'The war happened because of one assassination.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'The church declined because of one worship change.'
HowToRespond: Name the rest: 'Most big outcomes have many causes — let's name them.'

Definition: Treating mere possibility as probability — because something could happen, it is treated as if it will. Possibility alone sets no odds.
Example: Someone argues, 'This bridge could collapse, so we must never cross it.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'Someone could be offended, so we must never preach.'
HowToRespond: Ask the odds: "Possibility isn't probability — how likely is it, really?"

Definition: Rejecting a claim because you cannot imagine how it could be true. Our imagination is not the measure of reality.
Example: Someone argues, 'I can't see how evolution could produce an eye, so it couldn't.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'I can't understand the Trinity, so it can't be true.'
HowToRespond: Return to evidence: "Our imagination isn't the measure — let's look at the evidence."

Definition: Rejecting a real solution because it is imperfect, by comparing it with an idealized alternative. Perfect is not the standard; better than the alternatives is.
Example: Someone argues, 'This policy won't end poverty completely, so it's worthless.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'This church isn't perfect, so it's not a real church.'
HowToRespond: Reset the standard: "Perfect isn't the standard — is it better than the alternatives?"

Definition: Continuing a course because of what has already been spent on it, rather than what it will serve. Past investment does not make a bad course good.
Example: Someone argues, 'We've spent millions on this project, so we can't stop now.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'We've always done it this way for decades, so we can't change now.'
HowToRespond: Look forward: "Past investment doesn't make a bad course good — what serves the future?"

Definition: Judging people of the past as if they knew what we know now and had our options. Fair judgment starts by understanding their world.
Example: Someone argues, 'They should have known better in 1850,' without asking what was knowable then.
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone judges Old Testament figures as if they had a modern conscience and modern options, without first understanding their world.
HowToRespond: Understand first: "Let's understand their world first, then judge fairly."

Definition: Dismissing ideas merely because they are old, or assuming the new is better simply for being new. Age alone, in either direction, does not settle truth.
Example: Someone argues, 'That book is from the 1800s — obviously outdated.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'Ancient creeds can't speak to us today — they're too old.'
HowToRespond: Test the idea, not its date: "Age alone doesn't settle truth — old or new, let's test the idea."

Definition: Arguing that something is not so because it ought not to be so. What we wish were true does not change what is.
Example: Someone argues, 'The world should be fair, so this unfair outcome can't be real.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'God is good, so suffering can't be part of his plan.'
HowToRespond: Face the facts first: 'What we wish were true doesn't change what is — let's face the facts.'

Definition: Deriving an 'ought' from an 'is' — treating a description of nature as if it settled a moral question, or defining good in purely natural terms.
Example: Someone argues, 'Lions kill rivals, so killing rivals is natural and therefore acceptable.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'This behavior occurs in animals, so it must be morally fine.'
HowToRespond: Ask for the missing step: "What is doesn't by itself tell us what ought to be — that step needs its own argument."

Definition: Rejecting a distinction because no sharp line marks it. Vague boundaries do not erase real differences; clear cases still differ.
Example: Someone argues, 'There's no exact moment day becomes night, so day and night don't differ.'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'No sharp line marks when doubt becomes unbelief, so doubt and unbelief are identical.'
HowToRespond: Use clear cases: "Vague boundaries don't erase real differences — let's use clear cases."

Definition: Applying a concept to the wrong kind of thing, so the question itself is malformed. The error lies in the categories, not in the answer.
Example: Someone asks, 'What color is the number seven?'
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone asks, 'How much does God weigh?'
HowToRespond: Reframe the question: 'The question mixes categories — let's ask it in terms that fit.'

Definition: Treating an abstraction as if it were a concrete thing with its own will or weight. The abstraction is a way of speaking, not an agent.
Example: Someone argues, 'The economy demands sacrifice,' as if the economy were a person making demands.
FaithDiscussionExample: Someone argues, 'Sin is a substance you can wash off with enough effort,' treating a relational reality as a physical stain.
HowToRespond: Keep abstractions abstract: "Let's keep abstractions abstract — what do we actually mean here?"
